title: SYSK Selects: Virus Talk with Josh and Chuck
summary: SYSK Selects episode, introduced by Chuck Bryant, re-airing the October 2014 episode "Virus Talk with Josh and Chuck." The hosts explain what viruses are and whether they count as living, their structure (virion, nucleic acid, capsid, envelope), their shapes, how they infect host cells (hostile takeover, retroviruses, budding and bursting), the progression of colds and flu, contagious periods, latency and reactivation (HIV, herpes), fever as a defense, transmission routes, handwashing and soap, antibiotics not working on viruses, the age and evolution of viruses, vaccines, and the myth that mucus color reveals infection type. The episode closes with listener mail from Georgia Gilbert about churchyard burials and the plague, which the hosts note was bacterial, not viral.

entities.name: Virus Talk with Josh and Chuck

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this rerun pick from October 2014 on viruses. Josh says he is sick and wants to learn about the virus inside him, and the hosts joke about the topic.

segments.title: Are viruses alive?
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether viruses are living. A cell is the smallest living organism. Viruses cannot sustain themselves or reproduce on their own. One theory is that viruses are former cell fragments that became freelance renegades.

segments.title: Virus size, structure and virions
segments.summary: Viruses are about a millionth of an inch long, far smaller than bacteria, and can infect any living thing. A virion is an individual viral particle made of nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein capsid, sometimes with a lipid envelope. The hosts also cover the three basic shapes: helical, polyhedral, and complex.

segments.title: How viruses infect and hijack host cells
segments.summary: Viruses attach to host cells using matching proteins. Naked viruses inject genetic material, while enveloped viruses fuse with the cell membrane. Inside, the virus hijacks the cell's enzymes to make more viruses, which is described as a hostile takeover. Retroviruses insert their DNA quietly into the host's DNA.

segments.title: Colds, contagiousness and fever
segments.summary: The hosts walk through how a cold spreads from inhalation to nasal and throat symptoms, and when people are contagious: about a day before symptoms through several days after for colds and flu. They discuss fever as a defense that slows viral spread, and HIV and herpes as viruses that can lie dormant and reactivate.

segments.title: Transmission, handwashing and antibiotics
segments.summary: Viruses enter through inhalation, mucous membranes, or breaks in skin, and can be carried by vectors such as mosquitoes and fleas and survive on surfaces. The hosts explain that soap lifts germs off hands rather than killing them, and that antibiotics do not treat viral infections.

segments.title: Virus age, evolution and vaccines
segments.summary: The hosts say the oldest viruses tend to cause the least harm, since surviving hosts spread them better. Retroviral fragments are part of the human genome. Vaccines pre-expose the body to a virus, and they must be updated because viruses change.

segments.title: Mucus color myth
segments.summary: The hosts say the color of mucus does not reveal whether an infection is viral or bacterial, and call this an urban legend.

segments.title: Listener mail: Headstones
segments.summary: Listener Georgia Gilbert notes that churchyard burials grew from the practice of selling burial spots inside churches during the Middle Ages, and that plague years pushed burials outside. The hosts note the plague was bacterial, not viral.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and invite listeners to get in touch and visit the website.
